analysis.one_liner: Delays Medicare price negotiation for small-molecule drugs by four years, matching the timeline for biologics.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote, so Medicare's shorter 7-year negotiation timeline for small-molecule drugs stayed in place.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 2022 drug pricing law, Medicare can select a small-molecule pill for price negotiation 7 years after it was approved, but a biologic (an injectable or infused drug made from living cells) only 11 years after. This bill pushes the small-molecule timeline to 11 years too, giving makers of pills four extra years before Medicare can negotiate their prices. Supporters in the drug industry call the shorter pill timeline a "pill penalty" that discourages research; the bill's practical effect is that Medicare and its beneficiaries pay brand-name pill prices for up to four more years.
analysis.who_benefits: Brand-name drug makers, especially makers of widely prescribed small-molecule pills, keep exclusive pricing power for four extra years before Medicare negotiation can kick in, extending revenue on their biggest-selling products.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Medicare drug negotiation statute so a small-molecule drug is treated like a biologic: negotiation eligibility moves from 7 years after approval to 11 years [S2].

Four extra years of no negotiation on top-selling pills preserves several years of brand-name pricing on a large share of Medicare's highest-drug-spending categories, since most top-spending drugs are small molecules.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers. Beneficiaries face higher drug prices and premiums for longer, and the federal government forgoes some of the savings the negotiation program was projected to produce.

drawbacks.text: Delaying negotiation pushes back the day Medicare gets lower prices on widely used pills, which means higher costs for beneficiaries and the program for up to four more years on affected drugs [S2].

Supporters' best argument — that a shorter pill timeline penalizes small-molecule research and may steer investment away from pills — is an industry claim about future innovation incentives, not a documented present-day cost to patients; the tradeoff is unproven innovation against certain near-term higher prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's gain is a hypothetical research incentive; its cost is concrete and near-term: Medicare pays brand-name prices longer on many of its most-used drugs. Because the change is retroactive in spirit — it applies as if part of the 2022 law (Public Law 117-169) [S2] — it would also unwind planning already underway. The costs fall on ordinary beneficiaries; the benefits accrue to a concentrated group of manufacturers.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in two House committees all year, got sent to a health subcommittee in December, and died when the Congress ended without ever being debated or voted on.

narrative.text: Rep. Greg Murphy introduced the bill on January 31, 2024, joined by Reps. Davis of North Carolina and Guthrie of Kentucky [S1][S4].
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, and no markup or vote was ever scheduled in either [S4].
On December 17, 2024, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, a routine step that produced no further action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].
It drew 17 cosponsors — 15 Republicans and 2 Democrats — a modest showing for a bill that would substantially change the 2022 drug negotiation program [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, Medicare's shorter 7-year negotiation timeline for pills stayed in place, so beneficiaries and taxpayers avoided a four-year delay in negotiated drug prices; brand-name pill makers are the party that lost the chance to keep higher prices longer.

for.name: Rep. Greg Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to lengthen the small-molecule negotiation timeline from 7 to 11 years.

for.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA)
for.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned to repeal what it calls the IRA's "pill penalty" — the shorter negotiation timeline for small-molecule drugs — the exact change this bill would make.

against.name: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee consideration of the bill; it was referred to the Health Subcommittee in December 2024 and went no further.

against.name: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee consideration of the bill after its referral on the day of introduction.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and 15 of the 17 cosponsors were Republicans, with 2 Democrats joining; no vote was ever taken, so there is no roll-call to measure the split [S3].

industries.note: The bill gives them four extra years before Medicare can negotiate prices on their pill products, extending exclusive pricing on a large share of Medicare's drug spending. The cost of that delay is borne by beneficiaries and the program itself.
Equalizing the timelines would erase the relative disadvantage biologics currently face under negotiation, though no biologic's own timeline changes in this bill.
